1	---
2	title: The Graphic sub-tab
3	description: See which module draws a graphic clip, open it in your editor, and read what it reports when it doesn't draw as it should.
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';
8	
9	Select a graphic clip and the inspector's **Clip** tab gains a **Graphic** sub-tab. It's where you set what the graphic shows, see which module draws it, and find out what's wrong when it doesn't draw as it should.
10	
11	<AtAGlance where="Clip tab ▸ Graphic" tools={['set_graphic', 'get_graphic']} />
12	
13	<Shot
14	  name="07-clip-graphic.inspector"
15	  alt="The Clip tab with a graphic clip selected. Graphic, Picture and Clip sub-tabs sit above four sections. Source is collapsed and reads Lower third. Properties is open with six rows: Title, subtitle, accent, size, boxed and align. Size is collapsed and reads 960 × 540, and Timeline is collapsed and reads 00:00:05:00."
16	/>
17	
18	## The Graphic sub-tab
19	
20	A graphic clip's sub-tabs are **Graphic**, **Picture** and **Clip**, in that order. **Graphic** appears only when every selected clip is a graphic clip, so any other kind of clip in the selection removes it.
21	
22	| Section | What it's for | Summary when collapsed | Starts | Shows |
23	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
24	| [Source](#source) | What draws the clip, and what the module reports about it | The error or warning count, or the module's name | Collapsed | Always |
25	| [Properties](/graphics/properties/) | What the graphic shows | The number of properties | Open | When every selected clip is drawn by one module |
26	| [Size](/graphics/size-and-timing/) | The graphic's width and height | `W × H` | Collapsed | Always |
27	| [Timeline](/graphics/size-and-timing/) | The graphic's own timeline | Its length | Collapsed | With one clip selected |
28	
29	There's no **Color** sub-tab. To grade a graphic, put an [adjustment clip](/color/adjustment-clips/) above it.
30	
31	## The Picture sub-tab
32	
33	A graphic has the same layer settings as other clips, so you can move, scale and fade it: [Transform](/canvas/transform/) (position, scale, rotation and opacity), [Behind Subject](/effects/text-behind-subject/), [Hide While Silent](/effects/hide-while-silent/), [Shadow](/effects/shadow/), [Filters](/effects/filters/), [Reflection](/effects/reflection/), [Spotlight](/effects/spotlight/) and [Obscure](/effects/obscure/).
34	
35	It has no Crop, Corner Radius or Chroma Key, which are for clips drawn from media.
36	
37	## The Clip sub-tab
38	
39	**Clip** has the clip's [Timing](/editing/timing-section/) when one clip is selected, [Transition](/motion/transition-settings/) when the clip overlaps the one before it, and [Motion presets](/motion/motion-presets/).
40	
41	There's no Speed section. A graphic has no speed control or speed ramp, because its timing comes from the module and its [Length](/graphics/size-and-timing/).
42	
43	## Source
44	
45	Source says what draws the clip. Its summary, when collapsed, is `1 error` or `2 warnings` if there's anything to report, and otherwise the module's name.
46	
47	### Name, File and Revision
48	
49	| Row | What it shows |
50	| --- | --- |
51	| **Name** | The module's display name, or its file name when it has none |
52	| **File** | The module's file, `<name>.js` |
53	| **Revision** | The first eight characters of the SHA-256 of the file's text, which change whenever the text does, or `missing` when the file is gone |
54	
55	### Open in Editor
56	
57	**Open in Editor** opens the module in the app your Mac uses for `.js` files. Save there and the preview redraws within a moment. See [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/).
58	
59	### Reveal in Finder
60	
61	**Reveal in Finder** shows the module's file in a Finder window.
62	
63	Below these two, **Duplicate as New Graphic…** makes a copy of the module for the selected clips. See [Rename, delete and restore graphics](/graphics/manage-graphics/).
64	
65	## Diagnostics
66	
67	Under the buttons, Source lists what the module says about the clip, under a heading for each stage:
68	
69	- **Compiling the module** appears when there's something to report: the compile error, or any warnings the module gave as it loaded.
70	- **No errors or warnings at the clip's first frame** means that frame drew cleanly. **Checked at the clip's first frame** is followed by what that frame reported. Neither appears when the module didn't compile.
71	
72	The first frame is drawn at the clip's own size, so a missing font, a picture that isn't in the project or a size mismatch shows here. With several clips of one module selected, the check uses the first of them.
73	
74	Each row reads `line L, column C — message`, `line L — message` when it has no column, or the message alone when it has no place in the file. An error is in the stronger text colour and a warning is muted.
75	
76	While you drag a control, the list holds still. It updates when you let go.
77	
78	### Open a diagnostic
79	
80	Click a diagnostic, or its **Open** button, to open the module in your editor. This opens the file, not the line, so note the line number first.
81	
82	### In the graphics folder
83	
84	**In the graphics folder** lists what Frame Job skipped or couldn't watch when it scanned the project's graphics folder:
85	
86	- A module or picture with a bad name.
87	- An empty picture.
88	- A font that doesn't load.
89	- A file that couldn't be watched.
90	
91	Each row has a **Reveal** button, and clicking it or the row shows the graphics folder in Finder, not the file. These rows count as warnings in the section's summary.
92	
93	## A missing module
94	
95	When the module's file is gone, **Open in Editor**, **Reveal in Finder** and **Duplicate as New Graphic…** are disabled, **Revision** reads `missing`, and Source shows the error `No module named "<name>" in graphics/`.
96	
97	If Frame Job kept an earlier version, you can [restore it](/graphics/manage-graphics/).
98	
99	## Several modules selected
100	
101	When the selected clips are drawn by different modules, Source starts open and its summary counts them, such as `2 modules`. It names them and says:
102	
103	> Drawn by different modules: lower-third, title-card
104	>
105	> Select one module's clips to edit its properties.
106	
107	The rows, buttons and diagnostics are gone until you do. **Size** stays editable, because it doesn't depend on the module. **Properties** needs one module and **Timeline** needs one clip.
108	
109	## Switching clips to another module
110	
111	The inspector can't point clips at a different module that already exists. **Duplicate as New Graphic…** only switches them to a new copy.
112	
113	To move clips to an existing module, delete them and [insert that module](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/) again. An agent can do it in one step: [`set_graphic`](/mcp/tools-graphics/#set_graphic) with the clips and the new module's `name` draws them from that module, which must be in the project's graphics folder and compile.
114

1 --- 2 title: Graphic properties 3 description: Change what a graphic shows with its property rows, put values back to the module's defaults, and clear values the module no longer uses. 4 --- 5 6 import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro'; 7 import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro'; 8 9 A module decides what can be changed about a graphic, such as a title, a colour or a size. Each of those is a property with its own row in the **Properties** section, so you can change what a graphic shows without touching its code. 10 11 16 17 21 22 ## Property rows 23 24 Properties shows one row for each property the module defines, in the module's own order. A row's label is the one the module gives it, or the property's key when it gives none, and resting the pointer on the row shows the module's help text. The section starts open, and its summary counts the rows, such as `6 properties`. 25 26 Every row is a normal inspector row. A change is one undo step, and you can right-click a row's label to reset it. See [Inspector fields](/getting-started/inspector-fields/). 27 28 If there are no rows, the section says why: 29 30 | It says | What it means | 31 | --- | --- | 32 | "The module declares no properties." | The graphic has nothing to set. | 33 | "The module did not compile — see Source. Stored values are listed below." | Frame Job can't read the module's properties until it's fixed. See [Diagnostics](/graphics/graphic-tab/#diagnostics). The clip's values are kept and listed as [leftover values](#leftover-values). | 34 35 A module gives each property one of six types, and the type sets the control. The headings below use the names a module uses. 36 37 ### Number 38 39 A value field, with a slider beside it when the module gives both a minimum and a maximum. A number past the range is held to the end of the range. 40 41 The field shows two decimals when the module's step is below 1. With no step, it shows two decimals when the default or a bound has a fraction. Otherwise it shows whole numbers. 42 43 ### String 44 45 Text, in a one-line field the width of the inspector. Long text scrolls inside it. 46 47 When the module marks the property as multi-line, it's a text area instead: ↩ applies and ⇧↩ starts a new line. 48 49 A property holds at most 4,096 characters. 50 51 ### Boolean 52 53 A checkbox, for something that's either on or off. 54 55 ### Enum 56 57 A pop-up, for a choice from a fixed list. A module offers 1 to 32 options. 58 59 ### Color 60 61 A colour swatch. Click it to open the macOS colour panel. A colour you can see through keeps its opacity. Frame Job stores the colour as `#rrggbb`, or as `#rrggbbaa` when it isn't fully opaque. 62 63 ### Asset 64 65 A pop-up of pictures. It lists **None**, then every picture in the project's graphics, then any picture name that's referred to but missing from the folder. A missing name comes from the selected clips, the selected action's end or the module's default, so a missing picture still shows by name. 66 67 **None** gives the module no picture, even when it has a default one. 68 69 To add a picture to the list, choose **File ▸ Add Image to Graphics…** first. See [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/). 70 71 ## Reset 72 73 A **Reset** button appears on the section's header while a row differs from the module's default. Click it to clear every value stored on the selected clips, so the module draws its own defaults. It's one undo step, named **Reset Graphic Properties**. 74 75 To put back one row, right-click its label and choose **Reset to default**. 76 77 While an action is selected, the rows edit the action's end, not the clip, except a property the module marks `animate: false`. The header has no **Reset** then. It shows **Clear** once the action sets one of the rows, and right-clicking a row offers **Set end value to default**. See [Animate graphic properties](/graphics/animate-properties/). 78 79 ## Values at the default 80 81 With no action selected, setting a value back to the module's default clears it from the clip. The clip then follows the module's default if that changes later. 82 83 A colour counts as the default when its channels match, however the module spelled it. 84 85 The exception is a property an action on the clip animates. There, Frame Job keeps the default as a stored value, so the animation keeps its start. 86 87 ## Editing several clips 88 89 With several clips of one module selected, a change to a row applies to all of them, as one undo step. A row whose clips disagree shows the first clip's value with a **mixed** badge. See [Edit several clips at once](/getting-started/inspector-fields/#edit-several-clips-at-once). 90 91 Properties appears only when all the selected clips share one module. Clips of different modules can't be edited together, and an agent can't set their properties in one go either. See [Several modules selected](/graphics/graphic-tab/#several-modules-selected). 92 93 94 95 ## Leftover values 96 97 A clip can hold a value for a property the module no longer has, for example after you rename a property in the module. The value stays, listed below the rows with its key dimmed, its value beside it, and **⌫** to remove it. 98 99 The clip still draws. The value is passed to the module, and Source shows the warning `props. is not in the schema; it is passed through`. 100 101 **⌫** removes the value from every selected clip, as one undo step named **Remove Graphic Property**. 102 103 With no compiled module, every stored value is listed this way. An action's end has leftover rows of its own, marked as the action's. See [Animate graphic properties](/graphics/animate-properties/). 104 105 ## Good to know 106 107 A stored value that no longer suits its property, such as a choice the module has dropped from an [Enum](#enum), isn't listed as a leftover. The clip draws the module's default, and Source shows a warning naming the property. 108 109 ## With an agent 110 111 [`set_graphic`](/mcp/tools-graphics/#set_graphic) changes the same values, on any number of clips of one module, as one undo step. Setting a property to `null` clears it from the clips, except a property an action on the clip animates, which is set to the module's default. 112 113 ## Related 114 115 - [The Graphic sub-tab](/graphics/graphic-tab/) 116 - [Animate graphic properties](/graphics/animate-properties/) 117 - [Paste Graphic Properties](/graphics/copy-properties/) 118 - [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/) 119

2	title: "Animate graphic properties"
3	description: Use an action to move a graphic's numbers and colours over time, switch its text and pictures at a set moment, and keep some properties out of the animation.
4	---
5	
6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';
9	
10	A graphic's [properties](/graphics/properties/) can change over time, in the same way an [action](/motion/actions/) moves a clip's position or fades its opacity. Use this to slide a bar's size, change an accent colour, or swap a line of text part way through a clip.
11	
12	<AtAGlance
13	  menu="Clip ▸ Add Action"
14	  keys="⌥⌘K"
15	  where="Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Properties, with an action selected"
16	  tools={['add_action', 'set_action_end', 'set_graphic']}
17	/>
18	
19	## Animate with an action
20	
21	<Steps>
22	
23	1. Select the graphic clip, move the playhead to where the change should start, and choose **Clip ▸ Add Action** (<kbd>⌥⌘K</kbd>).
24	
25	2. With the action selected, open the **Graphic** sub-tab.
26	
27	3. In **Properties**, set the values the graphic should end at. Each row you change gets a ◆.
28	
29	4. Move the playhead through the action, or play it, to see the change.
30	
31	</Steps>
32	
33	<Shot
34	  name="07b-clip-graphic-action.inspector"
35	  alt="The Clip tab with action 1 selected on a graphic clip. The Graphic sub-tab and the Properties section each show a count of 3. The accent, size and boxed rows have a diamond in their gutter, and boxed says at end. The Size and Timeline sections show the ⊘ mark."
36	/>
37	
38	While an action is selected, the **Properties** rows edit the action's end, not the clip. A value you set is kept as you set it, even when it equals the module's default. **Size** and **Timeline** always edit the clip, and they show ⊘.
39	
40	The graphic gets the current values on every frame, and any animation the module does for itself still runs on top.
41	
42	To stop animating a property, take it out of the action. See [Set what an action animates to](/motion/edit-an-action/#take-a-property-out-of-the-action). To change when the action runs, how long it takes or its curve, see [Move, resize or remove an action](/motion/change-an-action/).
43	
44	## What ramps
45	
46	Numbers and colours move along the action's curve from start to end.
47	
48	**A number** arrives with decimals. Going from 64 to 129, it's 96.5 halfway, and it's never rounded or snapped to the property's step.
49	
50	**A colour** blends through OKLab, which keeps the middle of the blend clean, and its transparency blends as a separate value. `#ff0000` to `#0000ff` is `#8c53a2` halfway, and `#ffffff` to `#00000000` is `#63636380`, a half-transparent grey.
51	
52	While a property moves, every frame has to be drawn anew. A graphic that had settled costs a full draw per frame for the length of the action. See [Graphics playback and memory](/graphics/playback-and-memory/).
53	
54	:::caution
55	A module that needs whole numbers has to round them itself, or mark the property [`animate: false`](#stop-a-property-animating). One that does neither can fail on a fraction, and `new Array(props.count)` is the usual case. Those frames draw the error card, and an export stops there.
56	:::
57	
58	## What switches
59	
60	Text, checkboxes, pop-ups and pictures can't blend. They hold their value through the action, then change to the end's value as the action ends. Their rows say "at end".
61	
62	For a picture, choosing **None** in the pop-up means no picture from the end of the action.
63	
64	## Where an animated property starts
65	
66	An action starts from the value in force when it begins. That's the clip's own value, or what an earlier action finished on.
67	
68	If the clip holds no value for a property, the first action to name it starts from the module's default at that moment. That default is written into the clip in the same undo step, so changing the default later doesn't move the animation. A picture property with no default starts with no picture.
69	
70	Resetting the clip's own value for a property an action animates sets it to the default, so the action still has somewhere to start from.
71	
72	## Stop a property animating
73	
74	A module can mark any property with `animate: false`, and you can't then make an action animate it. It's for anything a ramp would break, such as a count, a layout mode or a data series. The bundled templates use it for counts and data series.
75	
76	The property's row shows ⊘, and it edits the clip even while an action is selected.
77	
78	If you write modules, it's one more key on the schema entry. It must be `true` or `false`, and anything else stops the module compiling. Leaving it out means `true`.
79	
80	```js
81	export const schema = {
82	  count: { type: "number", default: 5, min: 1, max: 20, step: 1, animate: false },
83	};
84	```
85	
86	See [The module API](/graphics/module-api/) or **Help ▸ Graphics Reference**.
87	
88	## Values and the module
89	
90	Each value you put in an action is checked against the module as it is now, including any minimum and maximum, and one that doesn't fit isn't accepted. That has a few effects when the module changes after you've animated it:
91	
92	- A value already stored isn't checked again, so narrowing a range later leaves the old end value in place.
93	- If an action names a property the module no longer declares, or no longer lets animate, the row shows dimmed with **⌫**. Choose it to take the property out of the action.
94	- While the module is missing or won't compile, the **Properties** section has no rows to edit, and reads "The module did not compile — see Source. Stored values are listed below." You can still take values out of the action with **⌫**.
95	
96	## The badge
97	
98	The **Graphic** sub-tab shows a **◆N** badge counting how many properties the selected action animates. The **Properties** section header shows the same count. See [Read the sections and sub-tabs](/motion/edit-an-action/#read-the-sections-and-sub-tabs).
99	
100	On the timeline, an action's band names a graphic's animated properties along with anything else the action changes, when the track is tall enough to show the label.
101	
102	## With an agent
103	
104	An agent works the same way. It calls `add_action`, then `set_action_end` with the end values as `{graphic: {props: {…}}}`. A property set to null comes out of the action, and `graphic: null` takes them all out. It never sends the module's schema, because Frame Job reads that itself.
105	
106	It can't set a value on a property marked `animate: false` that way, and sets it on the clip with `set_graphic` instead. See [Tools: animation](/mcp/tools-animation/#animating-graphic-props).
107

2	title: "Paste Graphic Properties"
3	description: Copy the text, colours and other properties of one graphic clip onto other clips drawn by the same graphic, and see what stays behind.
4	---
5	
6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	
9	Paste Graphic Properties copies what one graphic clip shows, its text and colours included, onto other clips drawn by the same graphic. Use it to give a run of lower thirds the same styling, then change the names.
10	
11	<AtAGlance
12	  menu="Edit ▸ Paste Graphic Properties"
13	  tools="paste_attributes"
14	/>
15	
16	## Paste graphic properties
17	
18	<Steps>
19	
20	1. Select the graphic clip you want to copy from and press <kbd>⌘C</kbd>.
21	
22	2. Select the clips to paste onto.
23	
24	3. Choose **Edit ▸ Paste Graphic Properties**. It has no keyboard shortcut.
25	
26	</Steps>
27	
28	Every selected clip drawn by the same graphic takes the copied properties, as one undo step. The menu item is on when there are Frame Job clips on the clipboard and at least one graphic clip is selected.
29	
30	## What moves and what stays
31	
32	The target ends up with exactly the copied clip's properties, so a property left at its default on the copied clip goes back to the default on the target.
33	
34	Each target keeps:
35	
36	- Its own module, size, **In** and **Length**.
37	- Its position, scale and everything else outside the **Properties** section.
38	- Any property the copied clip leaves unset and an action on the target animates, so that the action keeps its start.
39	
40	If you copied several clips, only the earliest one is read.
41	
42	## When it does nothing
43	
44	| What you'll see | Why |
45	| --- | --- |
46	| Some selected clips don't change | They're drawn by another graphic, or they aren't graphics. They're skipped. |
47	| A beep | The copied clip isn't a graphic, no selected clip is drawn by the same graphic, or the targets already match. |
48	| An alert | The copied properties can't be stored, for example more than 64 of them. It gives the reason, and nothing changes. |
49	
50	## How it differs from Paste Attributes
51	
52	**Edit ▸ Paste Attributes** (<kbd>⌥⌘V</kbd>) copies a clip's look, such as its position and opacity, and never carries graphic properties. The two are separate on purpose, because a graphic's properties hold its words as well as its look.
53	
54	| | Paste Attributes | Paste Graphic Properties |
55	| --- | --- | --- |
56	| Position, scale, opacity and other picture settings | Yes | No |
57	| A graphic's text, colours and other properties | No | Yes |
58	
59	See [Paste Attributes](/editing/paste-attributes/).
60	
61	## Copy a graphic clip
62	
63	Copying and pasting a graphic clip (<kbd>⌘C</kbd>, <kbd>⌘V</kbd>) pastes a clip that names its module. The module's `.js` file, fonts and pictures are not copied.
64	
65	So in another project without that module, the pasted clip draws the red error card. To fix it, add the module under the same name, for example with **From File…** in **Insert ▸ Graphic…** on a file of that name. **From File…** also places a clip of its own, which you can delete.
66	
67	See [Copy, cut and paste](/editing/copy-and-paste/).
68	
69	## With an agent
70	
71	An agent uses `paste_attributes` and has to ask for the graphic group by name, with `groups: ["graphic"]`, since it's never part of the default set. Unlike the menu item, a clip drawn by another graphic stops the paste with an error naming both, unless the agent sets `skip_missing` to skip those. See [Tools: copying and nesting](/mcp/tools-copy-and-nest/).
72	
73	## Related

76	- [Graphic properties](/graphics/properties/)
77	- [Animate graphic properties](/graphics/animate-properties/)
78	- [Copy, cut and paste](/editing/copy-and-paste/)

1	---
2	title: "Graphic size and timing"
3	description: Set the size a graphic draws at, fit it to the canvas, and control how its own animation runs when the clip gets longer, shorter or split.
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	
8	A graphic is drawn fresh at a size you choose, and it has an animation timeline of its own. The **Size** and **Timeline** sections of the **Graphic** sub-tab set both, so you can make a graphic sharp at any size and decide whether its outro follows the end of the clip.
9	
10	<AtAGlance
11	  where={['Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Size', 'Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Timeline']}
12	  tools={['set_graphic', 'add_graphic_clip', 'set_video', 'trim_start', 'trim_end', 'roll']}
13	/>
14	
15	## Width and Height
16	
17	**Width** and **Height** are the size the graphic draws at, in whole pixels from 1 to 8192 a side. The graphic's code lays itself out at that size, so text and shapes stay sharp.
18	
19	The **Size** section starts collapsed, and its header shows the size, for example `1920 × 1080`. With several graphic clips selected, a change applies to all of them, and a row shows mixed when they differ.
20	
21	A new graphic takes the size its [module](/graphics/what-is-a-graphic/), the code that draws it, asks for, or the canvas's size if it doesn't ask.
22	
23	The graphic is drawn at this size and then placed on the canvas like any other layer. Scaling the clip in the [Picture](/canvas/picture-tab/) sub-tab scales that finished picture. To make a graphic bigger and keep it crisp, raise **Width** and **Height** rather than the scale.
24	
25	Changing the [canvas size](/projects/canvas-size/) never changes a graphic's size. [Make Vertical Version](/graphics/vertical-graphics/) is the one exception.
26	
27	## Fit to Canvas
28	
29	**Fit to Canvas** in the **Size** section sets the size to the canvas's, then centres the clip at scale 1. It works on every selected graphic clip, as one undo step called Fit Graphic to Canvas.
30	
31	A graphic can't be larger than 8192 pixels a side, so on a bigger canvas Frame Job tells you why and leaves the clip as it was.
32	
33	## The graphic's own timeline
34	
35	A graphic counts its own frames from its first frame, separately from the project's timeline. The **Timeline** section shows where the clip sits on that count. It appears only when one clip is selected, it starts collapsed, and its header shows the length.
36	
37	| Row | What it shows | What you can do |
38	| --- | --- | --- |
39	| **In** | The graphic frame the clip's first frame shows. | Nothing directly. Trimming the front, rolling the cut before the clip and splitting all move it. |
40	| **Length** | How long the graphic's own timeline runs. | Type a timecode to pin it. |
41	| **Follow Clip** | Whether the graphic's timeline ends when the clip ends. | Tick or untick it. |
42	
43	### Follow Clip
44	
45	**Follow Clip** is on for a new clip. The graphic's timeline ends with the clip, so when you lengthen the clip its outro moves to the new end. Most graphics want this.
46	
47	Unticking **Follow Clip** pins **Length** at its current value. Ticking it again hands the length back to the clip.
48	
49	### Length
50	
51	Typing in **Length** pins it, which unticks **Follow Clip**, and is one undo step called Graphic Length. A pinned graphic keeps its pace however long the clip gets, so the animation doesn't stretch and its outro stays at the same point.
52	
53	The value snaps to a frame and can't be less than one frame. Typing the value the field already shows changes nothing, so untick **Follow Clip** to pin the length as it stands.
54	
55	### Length shorter or longer than the clip
56	
57	When **Length** is pinned shorter than the clip, the graphic keeps counting frames past it, but its progress stays at the end. What you see depends on how the graphic is written:
58	
59	- An animation driven by progress holds its end state.
60	- An animation driven by frame numbers keeps going.
61	
62	When **Length** is pinned longer than the clip, the clip ends before the graphic's timeline does, so a late outro never plays.
63	
64	## Trim a graphic like footage
65	
66	Trimming a graphic clip cuts into its animation, as trimming a video cuts into its footage. [Trim](/editing/trimming/) and [roll](/editing/slip-and-roll/) work as they do on any clip.
67	
68	| Edit | What happens |
69	| --- | --- |
70	| Trim the start, or roll the cut before the clip | **In** moves, so the animation starts further in. **Length** stays the same, so the outro keeps its timing. |
71	| Trim the end, **Follow Clip** on | The graphic's timeline ends at the clip's new end. |
72	| Trim the end, **Length** pinned | **Length** doesn't change. Shortening the clip can cut off the outro. |
73	| Drag the start earlier | A graphic has no source to run out of, so the start can go back as far as the track allows. **In** moves back and stops at 0. |
74	| [Split](/editing/splitting/) the clip | The second half's **In** moves, so it carries on where the first half left off. Both halves pin **Length** to the original's, which unticks **Follow Clip** on both and keeps the outro at the same point. |
75	| [Retime Range](/speed/retime-range/) | The clip stretches or squeezes like a title. A pinned **Length** stays as it was. |
76	
77	## Good to know
78	
79	- Actions can't animate size or timing. With an action selected, the **Size** and **Timeline** sections show ⊘ and always change the clip. See [What an action can animate](/motion/what-can-animate/).
80	- Adding a [transition](/motion/add-a-transition/) that gives a graphic clip extra frames at its head moves **In** back by the same amount, so the picture stays in step. Where **In** is shorter than the extension it stops at 0, and the graphic's first frame lands on the clip's new first frame.
81	- Changing the [project frame rate](/projects/frame-rate/) moves a graphic's own timeline onto the new frames. **In** and a pinned **Length** snap to the nearest frame. A graphic that counts in seconds keeps its pace, and one that counts frames runs faster at a higher rate.
82	
83	## With an agent
84	
85	An agent sets the size and the length with `set_graphic`, and can give a size to `add_graphic_clip` as it places the clip. A `length` of null is **Follow Clip**. To do what **Fit to Canvas** does, it sets the size with `set_graphic`, then the position and scale with `set_video`.
86	
87	No tool sets **In** directly. It moves with `trim_start`, `roll` and splits, as it does in the app. See [Tools: graphics](/mcp/tools-graphics/#set_graphic).
88

2	title: "Edit a module"
3	description: "Change a graphic's code in any editor, see the result as soon as you save, read what went wrong, and find the versions Frame Job kept."
4	---
5	
6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	
9	A module is the JavaScript file that draws a graphic. It's an ordinary file in your project, so you can edit it in any editor, and Frame Job redraws as soon as you save.
10	
11	<AtAGlance
12	  menu={['Help ▸ Graphics Reference', 'File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…']}
13	  where={['Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Source ▸ Open in Editor', 'Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Source ▸ Reveal in Finder']}
14	  tools={['get_graphic', 'write_graphic', 'restore_graphic', 'render_graphic', 'render_frame', 'graphic_reference']}
15	/>
16	
17	## Edit in any editor
18	
19	<Steps>
20	
21	1. Select a graphic clip and open the **Graphic** sub-tab of the **Clip** tab.
22	
23	2. Open the **Source** section and choose **Open in Editor**. The module opens in the app your Mac uses for `.js` files.
24	
25	3. Change the code and save. The preview redraws within a moment.
26	
27	</Steps>
28	
29	To use a different editor, choose **Reveal in Finder** in the same section and open the file from there.
30	
31	The file is `graphics/<name>.js` inside your `.framejob` project package, and **Reveal in Finder** takes you straight to it. Your own scripts and tools can write to that folder too, and fonts in `graphics/fonts/` and pictures in `graphics/assets/` are watched the same way. See [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/). The folder appears the first time something is written to it.
32	
33	A module's name is lowercase letters, digits and `-`, starting with a letter or a digit, and at most 63 characters. A `.js` file with any other name is skipped, and the **Source** section lists it under **In the graphics folder**.
34	
35	To write a module from scratch, see [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/) and [The module API](/graphics/module-api/).
36	
37	:::caution
38	Every clip drawn by a module changes when you edit it. To change one clip's look, use [Duplicate as New Graphic…](/graphics/manage-graphics/#duplicate-as-new-graphic) first.
39	:::
40	
41	## Live reload
42	
43	Frame Job watches the graphics folder, so you never reimport anything. When a module, a font or a picture changes:
44	
45	- The paused preview redraws.
46	- The inspector updates, including a property list the module's new code changed.
47	- A playing preview picks the change up on its next frame.
48	
49	Changes are gathered over about 100 ms, so a burst of saves lands as one.
50	
51	A save isn't an undo step and doesn't mark the project as edited. **Edit ▸ Undo** won't take your code back, but [kept versions](#kept-versions) will.
52	
53	## Diagnostics
54	
55	The **Source** section reports what the module says about the selected clip, grouped under headings. Its header shows the number of errors or warnings, or the module's name when all is well, so you can read it with the section closed.
56	
57	| Heading | What's under it |
58	| --- | --- |
59	| **Compiling the module** | The compile error, or the warnings the module's top level gave. |
60	| **No errors or warnings at the clip's first frame** | Nothing. That frame drew cleanly. |
61	| **Checked at the clip's first frame** | What drawing that frame reported, such as a missing font or a picture that isn't in the project. |
62	| **In the graphics folder** | Files the folder scan skipped (a bad module or picture name, an empty picture, a font that loads no face) or couldn't watch. Each has a **Reveal** button. |
63	
64	Each row reads like "line 12, column 4 — message". Click the row, or its **Open** button, to open the module in your editor.
65	
66	Every problem is one of two kinds:
67	
68	- An **error** means nothing drew.
69	- A **warning** means the graphic drew anyway.
70	
71	The line and column are the module's own, when they're known. Some things to know when reading them:
72	
73	- For a timeout, they point at where the function begins, not the statement that ran long.
74	- Some problems found while drawing name the frame in their message, such as "render returned undefined at frame 12 — did you forget `return`?".
75	- A warning from the module's top level, such as `asset("x")` outside `render` when `x` isn't in `graphics/assets/`, has no frame. It comes with the compile, and the module still compiles.
76	
77	**Help ▸ Graphics Reference** sets out the same rules under **Diagnostics**.
78	
79	The inspector only checks the clip's first frame. A problem that starts later shows up as the error card when the playhead reaches it.
80	
81	When the module file is gone, **Open in Editor**, **Reveal in Finder** and **Duplicate as New Graphic…** are dimmed, **Revision** reads "missing", and the section shows `No module named "<name>" in graphics/`. When the selected clips are drawn by different modules, **Source** names them and asks you to select one module's clips.
82	
83	## The error card
84	
85	A graphic that fails draws an error card in its own box, in place of the graphic. The card is dark red with a 2 px bright red border and white monospaced text. You'll see it in the preview and in stills.
86	
87	It appears for:
88	
89	- a missing module
90	- a module that doesn't compile
91	- an error your code throws
92	- a frame that runs out of time, which is 250 ms in the preview
93	- a frame whose picture can't be made
94	
95	The card reads, line by line:
96	
97	```text
98	lower-third · frame 42
99	render returned undefined at frame 42 — did you forget `return`?
100	```
101	
102	Its first line is the module's name and the frame, or `lower-third · does not compile`. The message follows, then a line such as `line 7, column 3` when the position is known. The frame number is the graphic's own, counted from its first frame.
103	
104	An error card never reaches a movie. An export [stops instead](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/#when-a-graphic-fails-partway).
105	
106	## Kept versions
107	
108	Whenever Frame Job sees a module's code replaced while the project is open, it keeps the code that was there. The last 10 versions of each module are kept.
109	
110	| Code is kept when | Code isn't kept when |
111	| --- | --- |
112	| You save from your editor | The file changes while the project is closed |
113	| An agent writes the module | Something other than Frame Job removes the file |
114	| You restore a version | |
115	| You delete the module | |
116	
117	The code the module holds now is never in the list, and code kept twice is listed once.
118	
119	To go back, choose **File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…**. See [Restore Graphic Version](/graphics/manage-graphics/#restore-graphic-version).
120	
121	Kept versions live in `graphics/history/` and travel with every save. Leave that folder to Frame Job. Fonts and pictures aren't versioned.
122	
123	## API.md and API.d.ts
124	
125	Frame Job keeps two files in `graphics/` for an editor or an agent working in the folder: `API.md`, the reference, and `API.d.ts`, its TypeScript definitions.
126	
127	They never create the folder. When the folder exists, Frame Job writes them as it opens the project and each time it writes a module, replacing either file if it differs from its own copy, so any edit you make to them is lost.
128	
129	**Help ▸ Graphics Reference** opens the same reference in your default Markdown app, with or without a project open.
130	
131	## How many files are watched
132	
133	Frame Job watches the graphics folder itself, its `fonts/` and `assets/` folders, and the first 16 files one by one: modules first, then fonts, then pictures, each in name order.
134	
135	That only matters in a folder with more than 16 files. An editor that saves by swapping in a new file is always seen. A save that rewrites a later file in place may not show until something else in the folder changes.
136	
137	## Good to know
138	
139	- In an untitled project, graphics live in a temporary folder and move into the package when you first save. A file you already have open in an editor is left at the old path, so choose **Open in Editor** again after saving.
140	- Saves less than about 100 ms apart count as one, so only the code from before the burst is kept.
141	
142	## With an agent
143	
144	An agent reads a module with `get_graphic` and writes one with `write_graphic`, or edits the folder with its own file tools. `write_graphic` compiles the code as it writes it and returns the result, so an agent sees each problem's level, message, line, column and frame straight away. A module that doesn't compile comes back as a list of problems to fix, not as a failed call. `render_frame` and `render_graphic` show it the error card and report what went wrong.
145	
146	See [Graphics with an agent](/graphics/agents-and-graphics/) and [Tools: graphics](/mcp/tools-graphics/).
147

3	description: "Rename a module and every clip follows, delete one no clip uses, bring back kept code, and copy a module to change one clip's look."

5	
6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';
9	
10	Each graphic in a project is a module, a file of code that any number of clips can share. These commands look after those files: rename one, delete one, go back to earlier code, or split a clip off onto its own copy.
11	
12	<AtAGlance
13	  menu={['File ▸ Rename Graphic…', 'File ▸ Delete Graphic…', 'File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…']}
14	  where="Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Source ▸ Duplicate as New Graphic…"
15	  tools={['rename_graphic', 'delete_graphic', 'restore_graphic', 'write_graphic', 'set_graphic']}
16	/>
17	
18	The three **File** items have no keyboard shortcut. Each opens a small sheet with a **Graphic:** pop-up.
19	
20	## Rename Graphic
21	
22	Renaming a module changes its file name, and every clip drawn by it follows the new name, on the timeline and inside nests.
23	
24	<Steps>
25	
26	1. Choose **File ▸ Rename Graphic…**. The sheet opens on the selected clip's module when one clip is selected, otherwise on the first module.
27	
28	2. Pick the module from **Graphic:** if it's a different one. The **New name:** field starts with the chosen module's name, and changes when you pick another.
29	
30	3. Type the new name and choose **Rename**.
31	
32	</Steps>
33	
34	<Shot
35	  name="15b-rename-graphic-sheet.sheet"
36	  alt="The Rename Graphic sheet. A paragraph explains that every clip follows the new name and how to rename back. Graphic: is a pop-up reading lower-third, and New name: is a field holding the same name. Bottom left, small grey text reads lowercase letters, digits and -. Bottom right are Cancel and a dimmed Rename."
37	/>
38	
39	A name is lowercase letters, digits and `-`, starting with a letter or a digit, and at most 63 characters. **Rename** stays dimmed until the name isn't empty and differs from the current one.
40	
41	The module's [kept versions](/graphics/edit-a-module/#kept-versions) move with it. If the new name belonged to a deleted module, the two sets of versions join under that name. Past 10, the oldest are dropped for good, and those are the deleted module's.
42	
43	The item is dimmed in a project with no graphics and while a nest is open, because a rename reaches every clip in the project. Leave the nest with <kbd>⌘↑</kbd> first.
44	
45	## Undo a rename
46	
47	When a clip uses the module, a rename is one undo step, **Rename Graphic**. **Edit ▸ Undo** puts the clips back and moves the module's file back to its old name with them, and **Edit ▸ Redo** moves both forward again.
48	
49	A module no clip uses makes no undo step. To go back, rename it again.
50	
51	Frame Job remembers the last 32 renames in a project to do this. An undo further back than that can leave a clip naming a module that has no file, and the clip draws the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card).
52	
53	## Delete Graphic
54	
55	Deleting removes a module that no clip uses. Its code is kept, so you can bring it back.
56	
57	<Steps>
58	
59	1. Delete the clips drawn by the module, or switch them to another one. See [Switch clips to another module](#switch-clips-to-another-module).
60	
61	2. Choose **File ▸ Delete Graphic…**. The sheet always opens on the first module in the list.
62	
63	3. Pick the module from **Graphic:** and choose **Delete**.
64	
65	</Steps>
66	
67	<Shot
68	  name="15c-delete-graphic-sheet.sheet"
69	  alt="The Delete Graphic sheet. A paragraph explains that a graphic clips still use cannot be deleted, that its code is kept so Restore Graphic Version brings it back, and that deleting is not an Undo step. Graphic: is a pop-up reading lower-third. Bottom right are Cancel and a blue Delete."
70	/>
71	
72	**Delete** is the only confirmation. There's no second question, and deleting isn't an undo step and doesn't mark the project as edited.
73	
74	Clips count wherever they are, on the timeline or in a nest. Fonts and pictures are left alone. The item is dimmed in a project with no graphics.
75	
76	## Switch clips to another module
77	
78	The inspector can't point clips at a different module that already exists. **Duplicate as New Graphic…** only switches them to a new copy. To move clips to an existing module, delete the clips and [insert that module](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/) again, or ask an agent to do it.
79	
80	## Restore Graphic Version
81	
82	Restoring puts back the newest kept version of a module's code, and it works on deleted modules too.
83	
84	<Steps>
85	
86	1. Choose **File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…**. The sheet opens on the selected clip's module when one clip is selected and that module has a kept version, otherwise on the first in the list.
87	
88	2. Pick the module from **Graphic:**. The pop-up lists every name with a kept version, and a deleted one reads like `lower-third (deleted)`. Under it, the sheet says how many are kept, such as "3 versions kept".
89	
90	3. Choose **Restore**.
91	
92	</Steps>
93	
94	<Shot
95	  name="15d-restore-graphic-version-sheet.sheet"
96	  alt="The Restore Graphic Version sheet. A paragraph explains that it puts back the newest kept version, keeps the code it replaces, and is not an Undo step. Graphic: is a pop-up reading lower-third, with 1 version kept in small grey type under it. Bottom right are Cancel and a blue Restore."
97	/>
98	
99	There's no list of versions to pick from. The sheet always restores the newest.
100	
101	The code a restore replaces is kept in its turn, and it becomes the newest. So restoring again returns to where you were, and the sheet swaps between those two rather than stepping further back. An agent can ask for any kept version.
102	
103	Restoring isn't an undo step and doesn't mark the project as edited. The item is dimmed when no version of any graphic is kept. For when a version is kept, see [Kept versions](/graphics/edit-a-module/#kept-versions).
104	
105	## Duplicate as New Graphic
106	
107	Clips that share a module all change when it does. This writes a copy of the module under a new name and switches the selected clips to it, so you can change one clip's look and leave the rest alone.
108	
109	<Steps>
110	
111	1. Select the clips to split off.
112	
113	2. In the **Source** section of the **Graphic** sub-tab, choose **Duplicate as New Graphic…**.
114	
115	3. Type a module name. The field suggests `<name>-copy`, or `<name>-copy-2` and so on when that's taken.
116	
117	4. Choose **Duplicate**.
118	
119	</Steps>
120	
121	Writing the copy can't be undone, but switching the clips can, as one step, **Duplicate Graphic**. Undo puts the clips back on the original and leaves the copy in the folder. Use [Delete Graphic](#delete-graphic) to remove it.
122	
123	The button is dimmed when the module file is missing. When the selected clips are drawn by different modules, **Source** doesn't offer it.
124	
125	## When Frame Job won't do it
126	
127	On success, a sheet closes without a message. When Frame Job can't do what you asked it beeps, shows the reason in the sheet in its own words, and the sheet stays open so you can change your choice or choose **Cancel**.
128	
129	| Item | The sheet says | What it means |
130	| --- | --- | --- |
131	| Rename | `graphic name "My Title" is not a module name…` | The name breaks the rule above. |
132	| Rename | `graphics/title.js already exists` | Another module has that name. |
133	| Rename | `The name "title" is already drawn by clip 4 on the timeline…` | Clips left behind by a deleted module still use that name. Delete those clips or switch them first. |
134	| Delete | `The graphic "title" is still drawn by clips 4 and 9 on the timeline and clip 12 in nest 7…` | The sheet names every clip that uses it. Delete them or switch them to another module first. |
135	| Restore | `…was changed outside Frame Job and no longer holds the revision in its name; it is not restored…` | The kept file doesn't match what Frame Job stored, so nothing is written. |
136	
137	**Duplicate as New Graphic…** reports the same two naming problems in an alert. Its clips stay as they were.
138	
139	## With an agent
140	
141	`rename_graphic`, `delete_graphic` and `restore_graphic` do what the sheets do, and give the same reasons when they can't. `restore_graphic` can name any kept version, not only the newest.
142	
143	An agent duplicates a graphic with `write_graphic` of the module's code under the new name, then `set_graphic`. `set_graphic` can also point clips at a module that already exists, which the inspector can't do. An agent can't rename a module while a nest is open either.
144	
145	See [Tools: graphic fonts, pictures and packages](/mcp/tools-graphic-files/) and [Tools: graphics](/mcp/tools-graphics/).

3	description: Save a graphic as a .fjgraphic file with the fonts and pictures it uses, and bring one into another project.

5	
6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	
9	A `.fjgraphic` file, called a package on this page, carries one graphic with the fonts and pictures it uses, so you can move it to another project or give it to someone else with Frame Job. Finder calls the file a Frame Job Graphic.
10	
11	<AtAGlance
12	  menu="Insert ▸ Graphic…"
13	  where={['Export… and From File… in the Insert Graphic sheet', 'A .fjgraphic opened from the Finder']}
14	  tools={['export_graphic', 'import_graphic']}
15	/>
16	
17	## Export a graphic
18	
19	<Steps>
20	
21	1. Choose **Insert ▸ Graphic…** and pick the graphic in the Insert Graphic sheet. It can be a bundled template or one from **This Project**.
22	
23	2. Choose **Export…**. It's dimmed when the chosen graphic doesn't compile, and while another export is running.
24	
25	3. A save panel slides down over the sheet, with the file already named after the module, such as `lower-third.fjgraphic`. Choose where to put it and save.
26	
27	</Steps>
28	
29	The Insert Graphic sheet stays open. The line under its lists says `Exporting <title>…`, then `Exported <title> to <file>:` followed by the files the package holds, or says why it couldn't.
30	
31	Saving over an existing file replaces it whole. If the export fails, the file already there is left as it was.
32	
33	Exporting changes nothing in the project and isn't an undo step.
34	
35	## What a package packs
36	
37	A package holds the [module](/graphics/what-is-a-graphic/#modules), which is the script that draws the graphic, and only the project fonts and pictures the graphic uses. To find those, Frame Job draws the graphic and packs what it saw used:
38	
39	- Every frame with the default properties. A graphic longer than 900 frames has 900 frames spread evenly over it.
40	- Then each other choice of each [Enum](/graphics/properties/#enum) property and the other value of each [Boolean](/graphics/properties/#boolean) property, one at a time, over up to 30 frames each. It tries at most 32 of these.
41	
42	A font is packed when the graphic drew or measured text with it, or fell back to it for a character its own font lacks. A picture is packed when the graphic's `asset(name)` drew it. The app's own fonts are never packed, because every copy of Frame Job has them, so a bundled template's package holds its module and nothing else.
43	
44	A frame that fails to draw is skipped.
45	
46	:::caution
47	[String](/graphics/properties/#string) and [Asset](/graphics/properties/#asset) properties are only tried at their defaults. A font or picture the graphic reaches only through another value, such as a different title or another picture, isn't packed. Read the file list in the message line after an export, and if something's missing, make it that property's default in the module and export again.
48	:::
49	
50	## The .fjgraphic file
51	
52	A package is a zip with nothing compressed. It holds `manifest.json`, the module, and the `fonts/` and `assets/` folders. The manifest gives the package's format, the module, its title, category and description, the Frame Job version that wrote it, and each file's path, name, size and SHA-256.
53	
54	Exporting the same graphic twice with the same version of Frame Job gives byte-identical files.
55	
56	A file name a zip path can't hold is stored under a tidied name. That covers a `:` or `\`, a control character and a leading `.`, so `a:b.ttf` is stored as `a-b.ttf`. The manifest keeps the original, so a font is still found by its family and `asset(name)` still finds its picture.
57	
58	A package can hold at most about 4 GiB and 65,535 files.
59	
60	## Open from the Finder
61	
62	Frame Job is the app macOS uses for these files. Double-click a `.fjgraphic`, open it with **Open With**, drop it on Frame Job's Dock icon, or open it from a browser's downloads. Frame Job [checks the package](#package-checks), then puts up the [Import Graphic sheet](#the-import-graphic-sheet).
63	
64	The package goes into the front project, the one whose window is in front. With no project open, it goes into a new untitled project. A package that fails its checks before the sheet appears shows an alert and opens no project.
65	
66	If Frame Job wasn't running, it opens first and the package waits until any projects it reopens are back, so it lands once, in one project, with no Welcome window.
67	
68	**File ▸ Open…** doesn't list `.fjgraphic` files, and there's no menu item for importing one.
69	
70	## Import with From File…
71	
72	<Steps>
73	
74	1. Choose **Insert ▸ Graphic…**, then **From File…**. The Insert Graphic sheet closes and a file panel opens.
75	
76	2. Choose a `.fjgraphic`. The [Import Graphic sheet](#the-import-graphic-sheet) appears for that same project.
77	
78	</Steps>
79	
80	The panel also takes a `.js` module, which goes straight onto the timeline. See [Insert a graphic](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/).
81	
82	## The Import Graphic sheet
83	
84	Before anything is copied, the sheet shows the graphic's title and description, then what will happen to each file:
85	
86	| Line | What it can read |
87	| --- | --- |
88	| Module | `Module: lower-third`, `Module: lower-third (already in this project)`, or `Module: lower-third-2 (lower-third is taken)` |
89	| Fonts | The font files, each plain, marked `(already here)`, or marked `(as Inter-2.ttf)`. With none, `Fonts: none`. |
90	| Pictures | The picture files, each plain or marked `(already here)`. With none, `Pictures: none`. |
91	
92	Under them it says "Importing copies these files into this project's graphics. It is not an Undo step."
93	
94	Choose **Import** to copy the files, or **Cancel** to copy nothing.
95	
96	If the project's graphics folder changed while the sheet was up and the import can't go ahead, Frame Job beeps, the sheet stays open and it says why.
97	
98	## Name clashes
99	
100	An import never replaces a file. Each file keeps the name the package gives it, unless that name is taken:
101	
102	| The project already has | What happens |
103	| --- | --- |
104	| A file of that name with the same contents | It's used as it is, and the sheet says "already here", or "already in this project" for the module. |
105	| A different module of that name | The module is copied under a new name with `-2`, `-3` and so on: `Module: lower-third-2 (lower-third is taken)`. |
106	| A different font of that name | The font is copied under a new name, such as `as Inter-2.ttf`. A font is found by its family, so its file name changes nothing. |
107	| A different picture of that name | The import stops, because the module asks for its pictures by name. An alert says so. Rename or remove the project's file and import again. |
108	
109	A name that differs only in case counts as taken. A module name also counts as taken while any clip still uses it, even when its file is gone.
110	
111	To find the project's pictures, see [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/).
112	
113	## After an import
114	
115	**Import** copies the files into the project's graphics folder and opens the Insert Graphic sheet on **This Project** with the graphic chosen, ready to insert. The line under the lists says what happened:
116	
117	`Imported Lower third as lower-third. Added: lower-third.js, fonts/Inter.ttf. Already here: assets/logo.png.`
118	
119	An import only copies files. It places no clip, so choose **Insert** when you want one on the timeline.
120	
121	Importing isn't an undo step and doesn't mark the project as edited. An untitled project keeps the files when it's first saved. If a copy fails part-way, what it had copied is removed.
122	
123	## Package checks
124	
125	Frame Job checks a package before it copies anything. If a check fails, nothing is copied, and the message reads `<file> cannot be imported:` followed by the reason.
126	
127	| What's wrong | What the reason says |
128	| --- | --- |
129	| The file is empty | `it is empty (0 bytes)` |
130	| It isn't a zip, or it's damaged | For example `the package is not a zip: no end of central directory record` |
131	| It was compressed, for example by zipping it again | `<entry> is compressed (method 8); a .fjgraphic holds stored entries only` |
132	| It was changed after it was written | The entry that differs from the manifest by path, size or SHA-256, such as `<entry> is 2048 bytes, but the manifest says 1024` |
133	| A newer Frame Job wrote it | `the package is format 2; this Frame Job reads format 1 — a newer Frame Job wrote it` |
134	| A font is bad | `the font "<name>" is not a .ttf or .otf file`, or why it doesn't load |
135	| A picture is bad | `the picture "<name>"` and why: it isn't a PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG or SVGZ file, its name can't be used, or it's empty |
136	
137	A module that doesn't compile passes these checks and is imported. It's listed on **This Project** with **Export…** dimmed, and **Insert** places nothing and shows the first error. Fix it the way you'd fix any module. See [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/).
138	
139	## With an agent
140	
141	`export_graphic` is **Export…**, writing to a path instead of through a save panel, and it also says how many frames it drew and how many failed. It writes nothing for an unknown graphic, a module that doesn't compile or a folder that doesn't exist. The assistant asks you before it runs, because it can replace a file.
142	
143	`import_graphic` is **Import** without the sheet, so nothing asks first. See [Tools: graphic fonts, pictures and packages](/mcp/tools-graphic-files/).
144

1	---
2	title: "Fonts and pictures in graphics"
3	description: Add fonts and pictures to a project's graphics, find the exact font name a graphic must use, and see why a font or picture doesn't draw.
4	---
5	
6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	
9	A graphic draws only with the fonts bundled with Frame Job and the fonts and pictures you add to the project, so it looks the same on any Mac. This page covers adding them, and what to do when one doesn't draw.
10	
11	<AtAGlance
12	  menu={['File ▸ Add Font to Graphics…', 'File ▸ Add Image to Graphics…']}
13	  tools={['import_graphic_font', 'import_graphic_asset', 'get_graphic']}
14	/>
15	
16	## Add a font
17	
18	<Steps>
19	
20	1. Choose **File ▸ Add Font to Graphics…**. It has no keyboard shortcut.
21	
22	2. Pick a `.ttf` or `.otf` file.
23	
24	</Steps>
25	
26	Frame Job copies the file into the project's `graphics/fonts/` folder, and every graphic in the project can then use it, straight away. Nothing is shown when it works.
27	
28	A file with the same name replaces the old one. If the file holds no font Frame Job can load, an alert says so and nothing is added.
29	
30	## Use the exact family name
31	
32	A graphic names its fonts in its code, and the bundled templates have no font property. So to use a font you've added, [edit the module](/graphics/edit-a-module/) and write the family's name in `font-family`.
33	
34	That name must be the one Frame Job reads from the font file, which can differ from the name Font Book or other apps show.
35	
36	If a font doesn't draw, select the clip and open **Source** in the **Graphic** sub-tab. Under "Checked at the clip's first frame" it reports the missing family and lists every family the project has, so you can read the exact name there. The section's header shows "1 warning" when there's something to read.
37	
38	The check looks at the clip's first frame only, so a font used later in the animation isn't reported there.
39	
40	## Bundled fonts
41	
42	These seven families draw on every Mac, with nothing to install.
43	
44	| Family | Weights |
45	| --- | --- |
46	| Anton | 400 |
47	| Bebas Neue | 400 |
48	| Darker Grotesque | Variable, 300 to 900 |
49	| IBM Plex Mono | 400, 500 |
50	| Montserrat | 800, 900 |
51	| Source Sans 3 | Variable, 200 to 900 |
52	| Source Serif 4 | Variable, 200 to 900 |
53	
54	## Generic families
55	
56	A module can also ask for a generic family, which draws in a bundled face.
57	
58	| Generic | Draws in |
59	| --- | --- |
60	| `serif` | Source Serif 4 |
61	| `sans-serif` | Source Sans 3 |
62	| `monospace` | IBM Plex Mono |
63	
64	Write a generic without quotes, as in `font-family="sans-serif"`. With quotes it names a family called "sans-serif", which isn't there. `cursive` and `fantasy` aren't available.
65	
66	## System fonts
67	
68	Graphics never use the fonts installed on your Mac, so a project draws the same everywhere. To use one of them, add its file to the project with [Add Font to Graphics](#add-a-font).
69	
70	What happens to a family name in a module:
71	
72	- A family the project doesn't have draws nothing, with a warning naming the families it does have.
73	- In a list such as `"Nope, Montserrat"`, the first family the project has draws.
74	- A family with a word starting with a digit must be quoted, as in `font-family="'Source Sans 3'"`. Unquoted, it draws nothing, with a warning.
75	
76	:::note
77	[Text clips](/text-and-shapes/fonts/) work differently, and do use the fonts on your Mac.
78	:::
79	
80	## Add a picture
81	
82	<Steps>
83	
84	1. Choose **File ▸ Add Image to Graphics…**. It has no keyboard shortcut.
85	
86	2. Pick a PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG or SVGZ file.
87	
88	</Steps>
89	
90	Frame Job copies the file into the project's `graphics/assets/` folder. A [picture property's](/graphics/properties/) pop-up then lists it, and a module can draw it by name with `<image href="${asset(name)}">`.
91	
92	A file with the same name replaces the old one. Any other kind of file can't be added, and an empty file gets an alert and isn't added.
93	
94	## Picture names
95	
96	A module refers to a picture by its file name, and some names can't be used that way. A name is not usable when it:
97	
98	- Starts with `.` or `#`.
99	- Holds any of `/ : " ' < > &`, or a control character.
100	- Is longer than 247 bytes.
101	
102	A picture with a name like that is added under a legal one, and a notice tells you which:
103	
104	> `"#logo&mark.png" was added as "logo-mark.png": asset(name) cannot use the name it had.`
105	
106	If the legal name is taken, the picture takes `-2`, `-3` and so on, as in `logo-mark-2.png`. A renamed copy never replaces an existing file.
107	
108	## Drop files in the folder
109	
110	You can also put fonts and pictures straight into `graphics/fonts/` and `graphics/assets/` with the Finder or any other tool. Frame Job notices within a moment.
111	
112	To find the folder, choose **Reveal in Finder** in the **Source** section of a graphic clip. It shows the module's file inside `graphics/`. If `fonts` or `assets` isn't there yet, make a folder with exactly that name.
113	
114	These are skipped, with a warning in **Source** under "In the graphics folder":
115	
116	- A font that doesn't load.
117	- An empty picture.
118	- A picture with a name a module can't use. Unlike a picture added from the menu, it isn't renamed for you.
119	
120	A file of any other kind is ignored, with no warning.
121	
122	## Good to know
123	
124	- Neither import is an undo step. To take a file out, delete it from the folder.
125	- Fonts and pictures belong to the project. Another project needs its own copy.
126	- Both menu items work as soon as the project window is open. There's no need to save first.
127	
128	## With an agent
129	
130	An agent can read the exact family names directly, rather than waiting for a warning. `get_graphic` lists them, and `import_graphic_font` returns the names a new file adds. `import_graphic_asset` can file a picture under a `name` you give it, and returns the name to use, including any legal name it had to choose. See [Tools: graphic fonts, pictures and packages](/mcp/tools-graphic-files/).
131

136	- [The module API](/graphics/module-api/)
137	- [Fonts](/text-and-shapes/fonts/)

1	---
2	title: "Graphics in exports"
3	description: "What an export draws for each graphic, what stops an export when one is broken, and where a graphic's warnings show up."
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	
8	An export draws each graphic the way the preview does, so the file matches what you saw. A broken graphic never reaches the file: the export stops and tells you which one and why.
9	
10	<AtAGlance
11	  menu={['File ▸ Export…', 'Window ▸ Export Queue']}
12	  keys="⌘E"
13	  tools={['export', 'export_status']}
14	/>
15	
16	## What an export draws
17	
18	An export draws each graphic as its module stood when you started or queued the export, whatever you edit next. Editing a module while an export runs doesn't change that file, and a job waiting in the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) draws the code it was queued with.
19	
20	So you can carry on working on a module while an export runs. To get your new code into a file, export again.
21	
22	## Parallel rendering
23	
24	An export draws its graphics ahead on worker threads, one fewer than your Mac's active cores, so a graphics-heavy export doesn't wait on one frame at a time. The file is the same as drawing them one at a time.
25	
26	It isn't used for an animated GIF or APNG, for a single frame, or for an audio-only export. Frames drawn ahead share the [memory budget](/graphics/playback-and-memory/#the-memory-budget) with the preview's.
27	
28	## When a graphic won't compile
29	
30	An export that would draw a graphic whose module is missing or doesn't compile isn't started, and any file already at that path is left alone. The message names each graphic and its first error:
31	
32	> The export was not started: the graphic "logo" has no module in graphics/; the graphic "title" does not compile — …. Fix the module and export again.
33	
34	The check covers every graphic clip in the export's range, and every graphic in each nest reached from those clips. That's the whole nest, not only the part the export plays, so a broken graphic elsewhere in a nest stops the export too.
35	
36	An audio-only export isn't checked, because it draws no pictures.
37	
38	A job in the Export Queue reports this in its row when its turn comes, and it keeps the code it was queued with. Fix the module and export again.
39	
40	## When a graphic fails partway
41	
42	Compiling is the only check made before an export starts. A graphic that throws at frame 900 is found at frame 900. A graphic that fails partway through stops the export at that frame, and no file is left behind:
43	
44	> The export was stopped at frame 900 of the graphic "title": … No file was written.
45	
46	The frame number is the graphic's own, counted from its first frame. A frame fails when your code throws, when your code takes more than 2 s on it, or when its picture can't be made.
47	
48	To find a failure before a long export, play the graphic through in the preview and watch for the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card). Your code has only 250 ms a frame there, so the preview is the stricter of the two. A frame whose code takes between 250 ms and 2 s shows the card in the preview and exports normally.
49	
50	## Warnings in a finished export
51	
52	Warnings a graphic gives while drawing don't stop the export. Frame Job reports each distinct one when the file is done, with the graphic's name and the first frame it happened on.
53	
54	- The Exporting sheet's finish line adds a count, such as "1 graphic warning (hover for details)". Rest the pointer on the line to see each warning.
55	- An [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) row adds the count too, and its tooltip lists them.
56	
57	Each one reads like `"title" at frame 12: message`. A warning given on every frame counts once, and an export reports up to 64 distinct warnings.
58	
59	## The frozen clock
60	
61	The clock inside a graphic is frozen, so nothing depends on when it's drawn and an export matches the preview. `Date.now()` is always `946684800000`, and `new Date()` is always 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z.
62	
63	A graphic can't show today's date on its own, so give it the date through a [property](/graphics/properties/). A date you write out in the code, such as `new Date("2026-03-01")`, works as usual. The rest of the sandbox is on [The module API](/graphics/module-api/).
64	
65	## Good to know
66	
67	**Save Frame** doesn't stop for a broken graphic. The graphic draws its error card, and the card is what's saved. See [Save Frame](/export/save-frame/).
68	
69	## With an agent
70	
71	`export` gives a broken graphic's reason straight away, before anything is queued. A failure while writing comes back from `export_status` as a failed job, naming the graphic and the frame, and a finished job lists any warnings under `graphic_warnings`, each with its name, frame and message. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).
72	
73	## Related

76	- [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/)

1	---
2	title: "Graphics playback and memory"
3	description: "How Frame Job keeps heavy graphics playing smoothly: drawing ahead, kept frames, Background render, and the memory they're allowed to use."
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	
8	A graphic is drawn from code, frame by frame, and a heavy one can take longer to draw than a frame lasts. Frame Job works around that by drawing ahead of the playhead and keeping what it has drawn. Nearly all of this is automatic, and the one thing you can set is [Background render](#background-render).
9	
10	<AtAGlance
11	  menu="Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Playback"
12	  keys="⌘,"
13	/>
14	
15	## Drawing ahead while playing
16	
17	While a preview plays forward over a project with a graphic in it, on the timeline or in a nest, Frame Job draws upcoming frames on spare processor cores ahead of the playhead. It uses one fewer core than your Mac has active.
18	
19	It starts again from the new spot on play, on a seek, and on an edit while playing. It runs to the end of the timeline, or to the end of the in and out range while playback is looping inside it.
20	
21	It doesn't run while the preview is paused or playing in reverse. Background render covers paused.
22	
23	## Kept frames
24	
25	A window keeps the graphic frames it has drawn in memory while it's open, so a stretch you play again comes from memory rather than being drawn again.
26	
27	A frame is matched by what it draws, so changing a module or a property only redraws the frames that come out different. Frames go when the window closes or newer frames replace them. The least recently used go first, and frames Background render drew ahead give way last.
28	
29	## Background render
30	
31	When you leave Frame Job alone, the window you last played or moved the playhead in draws its graphics ahead of the paused playhead, so the next play is smooth from the start.
32	
33	| Setting | What it does | Default | Range |
34	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
35	| **Background render** | Turns background drawing on or off. | On | |
36	| **Start after … seconds** | How long Frame Job must be left alone first. | 5 | 1 to 60 |
37	
38	Find them in **Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Playback**. They save the moment you change them, with no **Save** button, and they apply to every project. The ⓘ on the **Playback** heading explains them.
39	
40	Background render needs a paused window that draws a graphic. It draws from the playhead to the end of the timeline, or to the end of the in and out range while playback would loop inside it, and it ends early if the [memory budget](#the-memory-budget) runs out. After that it waits for your next activity and the same wait before it runs again.
41	
42	It keeps the processor busy while it runs, and it carries on while Frame Job is hidden or covered. It doesn't stop your Mac going to sleep. It only draws graphic frames, and it changes nothing in your project or your export.
43	
44	## Set how long it waits
45	
46	**Start after … seconds** takes a whole number from 1 to 60, typed or with the stepper. You can only change them while **Background render** is on. A typed number outside the range beeps and the stored value comes back.
47	
48	## What stops Background render
49	
50	Any activity in Frame Job stops the pass at once, and it starts again after the same wait.
51	
52	| Stops it | Doesn't stop it |
53	| --- | --- |
54	| A key, including a modifier key on its own | Moving the pointer |
55	| A click, a drag, a scroll or a trackpad gesture | Working in another app |
56	| Any edit, in any window | An agent's read-only call, such as `get_project` |
57	| Play, pause or a seek, in any window | |
58	| An agent's call that edits a project or moves a playhead | |
59	
60	It never runs while any window is playing.
61	
62	## The memory budget
63	
64	The frames drawn ahead and the frames kept share one budget for all of Frame Job. It's sized to your Mac, with no fixed cap in gigabytes.
65	
66	| Memory on your Mac | Budget |
67	| --- | --- |
68	| Normal | A quarter of its physical memory, so 8 GB on a 32 GB Mac |
69	| Short | An eighth |
70	| Critically short | Nothing. No frames are held, and each graphic is drawn when it's needed. |
71	
72	The frames an [export](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/#parallel-rendering) draws ahead count too. Frames being drawn ahead come first, and kept frames give up whatever room those need.
73	
74	Each playing window or export also holds at most 1,024 pictures ahead, however much memory is free.
75	
76	## What Frame Job skips
77	
78	Frame Job also avoids repeating work it has already done, in two ways.
79	
80	### Repeat frames
81	
82	When a frame's SVG is the same as one already drawn, such as during a hold or in a static graphic, Frame Job reuses that picture. Your module still runs for every frame. Only the drawing of its SVG into a picture is skipped.
83	
84	While an [action](/graphics/animate-properties/) moves a property that changes what the module draws, every frame comes out different, so a graphic that had settled costs a full draw per frame for the length of the action.
85	
86	### The picture cache
87	
88	PNG and JPEG pictures a graphic draws are decoded once and cached, so graphics full of pictures draw faster. The result is identical to drawing the original.
89	
90	The cache is a sixteenth of the graphics budget, so it shrinks when memory is short. The least recently used go first.
91	
92	## Good to know
93	
94	Your module's code has 250 ms to run for each frame in the preview. Past that the frame draws the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card). An export allows 2 s, so a frame that fails in the preview can still export. See [Graphics in exports](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/).
95	
96	Background render is a setting for a person. No agent tool reads or writes it.
97	
98	## Related
